sources.claim: A label associates an accessible name with its form control through nesting or matching for and id values.

canonicalExplanation.summary: Every form control needs a **visible, persistent label** tied to it: `<label for="email">` pointing at `<input id="email">`. The label gives the control its accessible name, and clicking it focuses the field — a bigger target for everyone. **Placeholder** text is not a label: it disappears when typing, is often low-contrast, and isn't reliably announced. Connect help text and errors separately with `aria-describedby`.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A sign-up form shows grey text "Email" inside each box — until you start typing, and it vanishes. Now which box was which? Screen-reader users may hear just "edit text". A label for=email points to one input id=email, while help and errors are connected separately. In this lesson you'll create a keyboard-operable form whose controls have persistent accessible names.

```predict
{"question": "An input has `placeholder=\"Email\"` and no label. What's the accessible name?", "options": ["Reliably \"Email\"", "Possibly nothing — placeholders aren't a dependable name, and they vanish while typing"], "answer": 1, "why": "Some tools use placeholder as a fallback, many don't, and sighted users lose it once they type. Always add a real label."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Paragraph and inline meaning**, **Relative and absolute URLs** and the **Form submission model** — every control needs a name to be sent.

sections.heading: The rule: one label per control, plus described-by for extras
sections.body:
```html

We'll send your receipt here.

Enter an email like name@example.com.

``` | Piece | Gives | |---|---| | `label for` = `id`. | the accessible name + a click target. | | wrapping label. | same, for checkboxes without ids. | | `aria-describedby`. | help and error text read after the name. | | real `button`. | keyboard: Enter/Space submits. | ```reveal {"prompt": "What's wrong with two inputs sharing `id=\"email\"`?", "answer": "ids must be unique. The label would point at only the first one, leaving the second unnamed."} ```

sections.heading: Keyboard check

includes: Pair every control with a visible label using for/id or wrapping.
Connect help and error text with aria-describedby and use real buttons.

outcomes: Create a keyboard-operable form whose controls have persistent accessible names.

examples.title: An email field with label, help and error
examples.situation: A label for=email points to one input id=email while help and errors are connected separately.
walkthrough: **Label for=email points to one input id=email:** the input's accessible name becomes "Email address".
**Help connected separately:** `aria-describedby="email-help email-error"` makes the screen reader read "We'll send your receipt here." after the name.
**Error:** when validation fails, the email-error paragraph is shown and read the same way.
examples.result: The email field has a persistent name, and its help and error messages are announced with it.

examples.title: The placeholder-only sign-up
examples.situation: A form's three inputs (name, email, password) have placeholders only. Users forget which field is which mid-typing; a screen reader reads "edit text, edit text, edit text".
walkthrough: No visible, persistent names exist once typing starts.
Assistive technology can't reliably name the controls.
Fix: add a `<label>` above each input with matching for/id; keep placeholders only for example formats, if at all.
examples.result: Every field is named on screen and to assistive technology at all times.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Placeholder text is an adequate replacement for a visible label.
misconceptions.correction: Placeholders disappear as soon as someone types, often have poor contrast, and aren't a reliable accessible name. Use a visible label connected with for/id, and connect help text with aria-describedby.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "The placeholder-only sign-up", what did screen-reader users hear?

analogy.example: A label is like a **name tag sewn onto a school bag**; a placeholder is a **sticky note** that falls off when you open the bag. You want the tag to stay for the whole year.
limitations: Bags don't talk; screen readers announce labels.
Help text is like a care-instructions label — separate from the name tag.

remediation.explanation: For each control ask: **What's its name if I hide the placeholder? Does clicking the name focus it? Is extra text connected with describedby?**

recap.summary: To create a keyboard-operable form with persistent accessible names, give every control a visible label via for/id (or wrapping), connect help and error text with aria-describedby, use real buttons, and never rely on placeholders as labels.
